en: Title: *Śatapañcāśatka* / *Adhyardhaśataka* / *Prasādapratibhodbhava* Author: Mātṛceṭa Source: Schackleton Bailey, 1951; input by Hartman at GRETIL
At all times, in every way, and in every respect, he in whom no faults whatsoever exist,
and in whom all virtues are established through their complete convergence. (1)

If one possesses discernment, it is right to go for refuge to him alone, to praise him, to worship him, and to abide by his teaching alone. Furthermore, those faults along with their latent tendencies do not exist in that sole Protector.
All [these] qualities are omniscient and they are imperishable.
For no one, even if intent upon the actions of mind, speech, and body, can find any opening in the Blessed One, for he is inseparable from the Dharma.
Thus, having attained this human state— a great festival of the True Dharma that is comparable to a turtle placing its neck through the hole of a yoke in a vast ocean—
and which is pursued by impermanence and fraught with the uncertainty of lapses in one's actions;
"How shall I make this Sarasvatī full of essence?"—
thus, although he has understood the countless qualities and subjects of the Sage,
an affection for only a single portion of them is undertaken out of respect for his own purpose.
Homage be to you, the Self-Existent One, whose deeds are abundant and marvelous;
for whom there is no certainty regarding his qualities by way of either number or power.
There is no end to them such that one could say "they are this many," so what talk can there be of them being "like this"?
We are merely talkative regarding virtues when it comes to saying "this is meritorious.
Having cast aside all deliberation as to whether something is endurable or unbearable,
you have yourself taken over this world which is now without a protector.

You are one who does not require the entreaties of the virtuous; you are affectionate without cause; you are a friend to those with whom you have no prior acquaintance; and you are a kinsman to those who have never served you.
You have even given away your own flesh—what need is there to mention other things?
O virtuous one, you have honored those who love you even at the cost of your own life.
You have purchased by the hundreds the bodies and lives of embodied beings from those who sought to kill them, using your own bodies as the price for their bodies and your own lives for their lives.

Neither out of fear of miserable rebirths nor with a desire for a preferred destination did you make ethical discipline your own; rather, it was solely through the purity of your intention. Through constant avoidance of the crooked and constant cultivation of the upright, [you attained this].
You have attained the state of being the sole path for the purification of karmic actions.
Though you were repeatedly oppressed, with a virtuous mind you revealed your inner splendor amidst afflictions and showed compassion toward suffering people.
The joy that arose in you when you were giving up your life for the sake of others—
that would not exist in living beings even if their lost lives were recovered.
[17] That which occurred when you were being repeatedly cut, regardless of the pain—
O Lord, even toward beings who would act as executioners, you felt compassion;
for you alone, O Hero, are the knower of the essence of that jewel-like mind which is the seed of perfect enlightenment, while other people remain far removed from it.
"The state that is difficult to attain is not obtained without performing difficult deeds";
thus was your vigor cultivated by you, regardless of your own self.
There was never for you a fixed limit to your extraordinary excellence.
Therefore, in you, the sequence of degrees among particular qualities has been severed.
Even toward very pleasant meditative attainments that bear fruit,
attachment did not arise in your heart, which is constantly bound by great compassion.
Happiness that afflicts those like you and does not favor them—
though it be refined— is not for you, O man of noble conduct, if it is shared with others.
Only that essence which is extracted from the mixture, entirely drunk and free from stain, is yours.
What you have spoken well has been avoided by you like poison, while what was ill-spoken has been rejected.
O knower of the essence of jewels, you have purchased the well-spoken word even at the cost of your life;
you have exerted yourself for awakening throughout those various successive births.
Thus, by striving in this manner for three incalculable eons,
accompanied only by your resolve, you have attained the unsurpassed state—
without harboring envy toward those superior to you, and without despising those who are inferior.
Without entering into competition with your equals, you have attained preeminence in the world.
Your attachment was directed toward the causes of virtue rather than their fruits;
therefore, through your correct practice, all virtues have reached their perfection in you.

In this way you have led your self to such a state of accumulation through your virtuous deeds that even the dust of your feet has attained the status of a sacred shrine. Having attenuated them, your faults were uprooted; having increased their merit, they were purified.
Through that well-guided practice of virtues, you have attained supreme perfection.
Likewise, you have struck at the faults with a total assault,
such that not even a trace of their latent impression remains within your continuum.
Having thus gathered and accumulated them again and again, you have instilled these qualities within yourself,
such that even a mere semblance of them is not seen elsewhere. They are subject to impairment and obstruction, limited in time, and localized.
Every worldly object used for comparison possesses some degree of excellence;
but what comparison can there be for your qualities, which are beyond duality, inaccessible, eternal, irreversible, and unsurpassed? (33–34)
The profundity of the salt ocean becomes as shallow as a cow’s footprint when it beholds the unfathomable and boundless profundity of your intellect;
the stability of the earth becomes as light as the tip of a *śirīṣa* flower’s filament.
When your steadfastness toward all phenomena has been made manifest,
O Sage, the sun does not find even the slightest ground within its domain compared to the light of your knowledge, which destroys the cataract of ignorance. (36–37)
The purities of autumnal moonlight, the sky, and water seem to attain a state of impurity in comparison to the purity of your speech, intellect, and conduct. By this,
everything that is virtuous in the world has been explained.
For the worldly ways of ascetics are far indeed from the qualities of a Buddha.
O virtuous one, you have attained preeminence solely through the acquisition of that very jewel of the Dharma;
by that alone is there equality between you and him.
But when something that is merely a deceptive pretense born of self-interest is introduced under the guise of a general or subtle principle, that is the excessive fickleness of the speaker.
For, reflecting upon the nature of dharma, I see it as being exceedingly subtle.
And this entire world has been won over by you toward the conquest of Māra.
For even when one is prepared to strike back with great fury,
there is no burden too heavy for patience, especially when it is established in a worthy vessel.
That very great destruction of the afflictions was accomplished on that very same night immediately following the defeat of Māra; that indeed is most wonderful.
It is like the dispelling of darkness by the sun, who is garlanded with a thousand rays.
O Hero, he would be filled with wonder at your victory over the heretics:
the passionate man by the one free from passion, the wrathful by the one who has conquered anger,
and the deluded by the one free from delusion— thus the three are eternally conquered by the three.
You praise the true dharmas and you censure the false dharmas;
yet for you, there is neither attraction nor aversion toward what is existent or non-existent.
You harbor no resentment toward the Arhats, nor do you feel attachment toward the heretics.
What praise could there be for you whose mind is of such a different nature?
You have no attachment even toward virtues, nor any craving even for those possessed of virtue.
Oh, how pure is your being, so perfectly serene!
Through the constant clarity of your senses, which never falters at any time,
your mind appears eternally serene as if it were before your very eyes.
From childhood onwards, the purity of your intellect and memory has been well known to all.
She was captivated by his well-spoken words and noble gestures, which were indicative of his inner nature.
To whom would this form—not tranquil yet lovely, radiant yet unassailing, restrained yet powerful—not cast its spell? (51–52)
Whether it has been seen by someone hundreds of times before, or whether one beholds it for the first time,
that form delights your eyes equally in both cases.
For your body possesses a quality that never tires the sight and a nature that is serene.
At every sight, she bestows ever-new delight.
Your body is endowed with the qualities of its substratum, and your virtues are endowed with the qualities of their presiding deity;
both are possessed of supreme excellence, each corresponding perfectly to the other.
Where else could these qualities of a Tathāgata be so well established,
except in this very form of yours, radiant with the primary and secondary marks?
Your form seems to say to those who have taken refuge in it, "I am blessed."
"Are we well-placed?"—as it were, his virtues replied thus.
(57) This entire world is bound without distinction by the afflictions;
you, however, have long been bound by compassion for the sake of liberating the world from its afflictions. (58)

Whom indeed should I first revere: you, or Great Compassion, by which you—though knowing such faults—have remained for so long in saṃsāra? For even though you have become habituated to the bliss of discernment, those [faults] have passed away from you as you were beset by them.
That which has been done by you through compassion, having found its opportunity at the right time, is indeed like this:
from the peaceful forest, you are drawn toward the edge of the village out of compassion for those to be trained, just as an elephant is drawn from a lake by means of a magic spell.

Although you abide in supreme tranquility, being moved by the power of compassion, you have even set foot upon the arts of the actors and musicians. Whatever supernatural powers you possess, whatever lion’s roars you utter, and whatever manifestations of your own virtues there may be—

For you, whose mental activity has cast out all desire, that compassion is the touchstone of your virtue. O Lord, although your compassion— which is solely and exclusively for the welfare of others— is indeed harsh toward its own locus,
it became truly compassionate only in you.
For indeed, having divided you into a hundred parts like an offering for some purpose, the wise ones have scattered you throughout the quarters for the sake of accomplishing the aims of others. Yet,
it is clearly by your own will that she proceeds in accordance with them.
For even though she contradicts you, she, being virtuous, does not commit an offense.
(66) Her words are well-phrased, of great significance, truthful, and sweet;
they possess both hidden and manifest meanings, and are characterized by both conciseness and elaboration. (67)
Upon hearing such words as these of yours, who would not be convinced that you are omniscient, even if they were previously skeptical?
For almost everything is sweet [to the ear], and only by necessity is anything otherwise.
Indeed, every single word of yours is well-spoken through the accomplishment of your purpose.
Whether it be gentle, harsh, or endowed with both qualities, all your speech attains a single flavor upon reflection. (69–70)
Oh, how supreme is the skill of these perfectly pure deeds,
by which this vessel for such jewels of speech has been fashioned!
For from this, which is beautiful to the eye, comes that which is enchanting to the ear.
From your mouth flows forth speech like nectar flowing from the moon.
Your speech acts as a rain-cloud, pacifying the dust of passion;
it acts as Garuḍa in the matter of extracting the serpent of hatred.
It acts as the sun once again, dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
it acts as Indra’s weapon, utterly cleaving the mountains of pride.
Because its object is directly perceived, it is unerring; because it is free from afflictions, it is undisturbed.
For your speech is indeed "threefold auspicious" because it is well-composed and possesses the power of persuasion.
First, your words captivate the minds of the listeners;
then, when they are reflected upon, they dispel both passion and darkness.

Your speech brings consolation to those in distress and terror to the heedless; it inspires spiritual urgency in those who are comfortable. It generates joy for the wise and increases the intelligence of those of middling capacity.
This speech of yours is a destroyer of darkness for the dull-witted and is beneficial to all people.
It draws away [beings] from [false] views and draws them toward Nirvana;
it extracts faults and rains down virtues.

Your intellect is unimpeded everywhere, your mindfulness is ever-present, and thus every prediction you make is unfailing in all circumstances. For you do not act in an improper place, at an improper time, nor toward an unworthy recipient.
Because you have exerted effort correctly, your word is unfailing.

Your teaching alone—leading to the single goal, easy to practice, bringing its own results, free from calamity, and virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end—is not found in any other [teaching]. (81–82)

Thus, because of their attachment to views, those fools despise your doctrine, which is so exceedingly beautiful; yet there is no enemy equal to dogmatic views. For the sake of this [doctrine], you have endured the many calamities of the world.
Therefore, remembering that, you should remain steadfast even in adversity within the teaching;
how much more so, then, should the teaching of one who acts for your benefit and speaks for your benefit not be carried out by you, even if your head were on fire? (84–85)
Freedom from bondage, the bliss of awakening, the honoring of your virtues, and tranquility—
all this fourfold excellence is attained through your teaching.
It is a terror to all non-Buddhist teachers and a torment to Namuci.
O Hero, this command of yours is a source of consolation for the gods among men.
This great domain of the three realms—unattached and unrestrained—is pervaded by your command, even the command of Death himself. (87–88)
For one who knows the method of your teaching may remain even for an eon by his own will;
yet, being independent, he goes to that place where death has no domain.
[This applies] to the contemplation of the meaning of the scripture and to the cultivation of worship.

The distinction between the three times exists nowhere else but in your teaching. O bull among sages, what indeed could be more calamitous than this, that they do not honor this teaching of yours, which is so richly endowed with excellence? (90–91)
Hearing you brings satisfaction; seeing you brings clarity;
your speech gladdens; your teaching liberates.
Your birth inspires joy; your growth delights all beings.
Engagement bestows grace, while withdrawal strikes down [evil].
(93) Recitation removes sin; remembrance of you brings joy;
seeking you sharpens the intellect; and full knowledge brings purification. (94)
Approaching you brings prosperity; serving you brings supreme wisdom;
worshipping you brings fearlessness; and attending upon you brings auspiciousness. Purified by the perfection of virtuous conduct, one becomes serene through the perfection of meditation.
You are an unshakeable lake of perfect wisdom, a great reservoir composed of merit.
Your form is a jewel to be beheld; your well-spoken words are a jewel to be heard;
the Dharma is a jewel for investigation—for you are indeed a mine of jewels of virtue.
You are an island for those being swept away by the floods, a protection for those whose selves are wounded,
a refuge for those fearing worldly existence, and the ultimate resort for those seeking liberation.
You are a worthy recipient because of your pure conduct, and a fertile field because of the abundance of your fruit.
Because you act for their welfare, you are a true friend to all living beings.
Because you are affectionate, you are helpful; because you are delightful, you are captivating.
Because of your gentleness, you are uniquely lovely and highly esteemed by all for your many virtues.

You are dear to the heart because you are irreproachable; you are delightful because of the excellence of your speech and form; you are blessed because all your aims are accomplished; and you are auspicious because you are the refuge of all virtues.
You are the one who casts aside those who persist in error and the restrainer of those who take away [merit].
You are the restorer of those who have gone astray and the inspirer of those who move sluggishly;
you are the driver of those who are tamed to the yoke and the one who overlooks the wild horses.
Therefore, among those to be tamed by men, you are the unsurpassed and true charioteer. (102–103)

Compassion for those in distress, a desire for their welfare when they are healthy, sympathy for those in calamity, and a wish for the benefit of all; affection even toward those who oppose you, and an inclination even toward those who have fallen. 104.

Compassion even toward those who are fierce—what indeed is this nobility of yours? If it is claimed that parents possess the status of "guru" because of their beneficence, then what kind of "guru-status" could there be for you, who have been so exceedingly beneficial? 105–106.
Like selfs that are opposed to one another and indifferent to their own interests, you have become a rampart for those standing on the edge of a precipice;
for the benefit of both worlds and for transcending the world. (107)
In worlds that had become shrouded in darkness, the light of wisdom was created by you.
The modes of enjoyment of gods and humans were divided;
yet, through the commonality of the enjoyment of the Dharma, they have come to find non-distinction in you.
O Blessed One, you have indeed extended this universal hospitality toward all phenomena, regardless of their mode of birth, age, color, place, or time.
You treat those who are unimpressed as if they were impressed, and you inspire longing in those who are free from longing.
Those gods wait upon even the disciples with palms joined in reverence.
Oh, how radiant is the arising of a Buddha, the ornament of cyclic existence,
wherein even the state of being human has become an object of longing for the gods!
Weariness, the loss of the bliss of tranquility, association with the wicked, the pairs of opposites, and being crowded— bearing these faults as virtues,
you strive for the welfare of the world with an unattached mind. (113)
What indeed is this blessed nature of the Buddhas?
(114) Even poor food was eaten at times, hunger was endured, uneven paths were traversed, and sleep was sought even upon thorns. (115)
O Lord, even though you are the Sovereign, out of affection for those to be trained, you have undergone delays, concealment, service, and assumed various dress and speech; yet, O Lord,
even this sovereignty is never found within yourself.
For you are indeed employed at your own will by everyone for their own purposes as if you were meant to speak;
yet, however you are urged by anyone, anywhere, or in any manner, you do not overstep your own auspicious course of conduct. (117–118)
People do not act with such devotion toward one intent on helping as you act toward one intent on harming;
nor are they such devoted friends to an enemy intent on their ruin as you are to one intent on their welfare.
Even though you were constantly intent on seeking out faults, you were devoted to seeking out virtues.
Since your invitation was accompanied by poison and fire,
your journey there was full of compassion and like nectar.

Abusers were conquered by you through patience; those who sought to do you harm through blessings; slanderers through truth; and those who wished to kill through loving-kindness. The many innate dispositions of men, which have been suppressed since beginningless time— [122]
The calamities manifested by you were overturned in an instant:
that the harsh became gentle, the miserly became generous, and the cruel attained kindness—that is your skill in means. (123–124)
The pacification of the senses in Nanda, the humility of Mānastabdha, and the forbearance of Aṅgulimāla—whom would these not fill with wonder?
Many have abandoned golden beds to sleep upon beds of grass. (125)
Those steadfast ones, satiated with the essence of Dharma, lay down in comfort.
Though questioned, you said nothing; though approached, you did not engage in conversation.
Having quenched their thirst for the truth, you spoke of the next world, O knower of the proper time and disposition.

Having first produced excellence in the mind through discourses on generosity and the like, the Dharma was then imparted, like dye upon a cloth free from stains. There is no means or power by which you have not exerted yourself.
To uplift the wretched world from the terrible abyss of saṃsāra,
many words and deeds of manifold forms have been manifested by you in various places, according to the differing dispositions of those to be trained. (129–130)
All these [deeds] are pure, uncontradicted, honored, and revered;
they are beneficial and magnanimous for all gods and men.
Indeed, it is not possible to speak or perform much that is both good and right.
Both speaking otherwise and not otherwise are seen in you.
By the purity of your self alone, the world would become purified;
for no such field exists within the three worlds as this.
How much more so for those who have utterly perished throughout the beginningless turmoil of existence!
You alone are thus exerted for the benefit of all sentient beings.
I know of no path by which your debt of gratitude could ever be repaid.
Even those who attain final nirvāṇa remain your debtors;
for they abide in your Dharma and accomplish only their own self-interest. As for the labor they exert for that purpose, what recompense can there be for you? (135–136)

For you remain awake, observing the continuums of those who sleep; vigilant among the heedless beings, you are a kinsman of auspiciousness. The destruction of the afflictions has been proclaimed, and the illusion of Māra has been dispelled.
The wretchedness of cyclic existence has been described, and the direction of fearlessness has been shown.
What else remains for one who desires the welfare of beings and is compassionate toward them, such that you would not grant your assent to it? (138–139)
If these phenomena were migratory, they would certainly have been established by you everywhere, taking Devadatta as their basis.
For this very reason, O Lord of the World, here one thing is not the agent of another.
Thus you have spoken, as if making the world understand its true nature:
having long since impelled the True Dharma upon the earth out of compassion for the world,
and having produced many excellent disciples capable of bestowing grace upon the three realms.
Having directly disciplined the assembly of those to be trained, ending with Subhadra,
what debt toward sentient beings still remains for you today—
that you, grinding your bones into pieces as small as sesame seeds with the vajra of meditative concentration? (143)
Even at the very end, you did not cease from performing what is exceedingly difficult to do.
You have demonstrated to this world, which is so difficult to instruct, that both the Dharma-body and the Form-body exist solely for the sake of others— even in your Nirvana.
For thus, having transmitted the Dharma-body in its entirety to those worthy of it, and having broken your form-body into pieces as small as sesame seeds, you have entered final nirvāṇa.
Oh, what a state! Oh, what conduct! Oh, what beauty! Oh, what virtues!
Indeed, there is nothing at all that is not wondrous among the qualities of a Buddha.
Yet, even toward you—who are beneficial, pleasing to the eye, and whose speech and bodily actions are peaceful—people show hostility; behold the ferocity of delusion! 147–148
To those beings who pay homage to you— the ocean of merit, the treasury of jewels, the mass of Dharma, and the mine of virtues— to them also I offer my salutation.
O Protector, your qualities are inexhaustible, whereas my power is limited.
Therefore, one remains out of fear of falling into error, not out of a sense of satiety.
[150] You alone are worthy of knowing yourself by yourself—immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and invisible. [151]
Not even a fraction of a portion of your virtues has been proclaimed, yet supreme satisfaction remains in our hearts;
for the waters of great lakes do not diminish by being drawn out.
The thirsts of people indeed go to pacification through the arising of the fruit of this auspicious karma of mine,
which was born from the inspired intuition granted by the grace of the Sage.
May the mind of all beings, driven by the wind of unwholesome thoughts, come under control. || 153 ||
